title: Crypto Series Wrap-up
subtitle: Primes, key recovery and certificates
description: Steve and Leo finish their crypto series: how many primes there are, how hard factoring really is, how organizations recover lost private keys by splitting secrets among trustees, and what a security certificate actually is.

beats.t: Episode 37, recorded over lunch in Toronto while we tape Call for Help. For once I'm sitting across from you.
A listener who works at the CIA wrote that people looked at him funny. He was giggling walking through security at headquarters, after the Diffie-Hellman episode clicked for him.

Speaking of Langley: the Kryptos sculpture there has four encrypted sections. Three were solved in 1999, and the fourth has resisted everyone for 16 years. Now sculptor Jim Sanborn says he made a mistake: an extra X, put in for aesthetic reasons. It changes a few words of the third section.

beats.title: Kryptos
beats.t: Kryptos was installed at CIA headquarters in 1990, with encryption help from retired CIA cryptographer Ed Scheidt. In April 2006, Sanborn said he had left out an X in the second section, not the third as said on the show. Restoring it changed that section's ending. The fourth section has resisted public solution for decades.
Today we tie up the loose ends: stream ciphers, block ciphers, public key and hashes are covered. Now primes, key recovery and certificates.

chapters.title: Why Not a Table of Primes?

beats.t: First loose end: primes. Listeners asked, if primes are rare, why not precompute all of them and try each one?
In a 10-by-10 grid of the first hundred numbers, only a couple of dozen are prime.
Primes feel rare, but magnitudes fool us. There are more primes of 512 bits or fewer than there are atoms in the known universe.
You can't print a book that big, and you couldn't search it if you did.

beats.title: The prime number theorem
beats.t: The number of primes below N is roughly N divided by the natural log of N. Below 2^512 that's about 2^503, around 10^151 primes. The observable universe has an estimated 10^80 atoms.
A 1,024-bit RSA key is the product of two 512-bit primes. Multiply two binary numbers and their lengths add.
I use 4,096 bits, but let's stay with 1,024.
So how hard is factoring? Diffie-Hellman's one-way function is exponentiation. RSA's is multiplication. Reversing it is factoring: find the two primes. Know either one and you just divide.
The record I found: a 512-bit number, two 256-bit primes, took a team with 292 off-the-shelf PCs five months to factor.
Brute-forcing a symmetric key doubles in difficulty with each added bit. Factoring doesn't. Each bit makes it only about 1.035 times harder.
But compound that 512 more times, up to 1,024 bits, and you're at somewhere between 3 and 30 million years with current technology.
So if it's ever cracked, it won't be by brute force. It'll be a mathematical breakthrough.
Or someone finding the slip of paper you wrote your passphrase on.
Couldn't someone at the NSA have found a better way?
That's why cryptographers always say "believed to be secure," or "as far as we know."
Still, this is mathematics people have worked on since Eratosthenes.

beats.title: Factoring records since
beats.t: RSA-155, a 512-bit number, was factored in 1999 using about 300 computers. RSA-768 fell in 2009, and an 829-bit number in 2020. Improved algorithms and hardware mean 1,024-bit RSA is no longer considered safe. NIST has required at least 2,048 bits since 2013.

beats.title: The quantum caveat
beats.t: A large enough quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could factor RSA keys and break Diffie-Hellman efficiently. None exists yet, but NIST published post-quantum standards in 2024, and browsers have begun adopting them.
Next loose end: key recovery. You keep your private key private. But what if you lose it? Your hard drive crashes, or your token goes missing.
I've made about eight keys over the years and lost all but the last couple. I can't even revoke the old ones.
Though a bad guy who gets my key still needs my passphrase.
True, but here the danger is losing it yourself. People can still send you messages you can't decrypt, and you can't sign anything.

A company that issues keys to every employee wants a safe store of them: key recovery. But like the two officers on a submarine who both have to turn their keys, you don't want one person able to unlock them all.
Idea one: encrypt the key database with a random 128-bit key and give two people 64 bits each. But now each person only needs to find 64 more bits, which can be brute-forced.
And if one is in Tahiti on vacation, you're stuck. So try two-of-three: split the key into three parts, and give each person two of them.
Now each piece is only about 43 bits, and 40-bit keys have already been cracked.
So we scrap the whole idea.
The solution is a toe-curling concept. Two points define a line. Draw a line on an x-y grid, and let the place it crosses the y-axis be the key.
Give each trustee one point on that line. One point alone tells you nothing, since infinitely many lines pass through it.
They can rotate around that point.
But any two trustees together define the line, and so the key. And you can hand out as many points as you like.
What if you want to require three people?
Three points define a parabola. Two points leave a whole family of parabolas, but a third nails it down.
And four?
It generalizes to curves of any order. It's simple polynomial math, and you can set any policy: how many trustees, and how many must come together.

beats.title: Shamir's Secret Sharing
beats.t: Adi Shamir, the S in RSA, published this in 1979. To require k of n people, choose a random polynomial of degree k−1 whose value at zero is the secret, and give each person one point. Any k points reveal the secret, and fewer reveal nothing at all. Real systems do the math in a finite field rather than on a real-number grid.
Last loose end: certificates. A listener says Thawte still offers free personal certificates, though for shorter periods.

beats.title: Free email certificates
beats.t: Thawte stopped issuing its free personal email certificates in 2009. Free S/MIME certificates are still available from some providers, and Let's Encrypt has issued free HTTPS certificates since 2015.
S/MIME, Secure MIME, is built into email clients like Outlook Express. Add your certificate and those of your correspondents, and mail can be encrypted automatically. We'll do a whole episode on it.
The problem with public keys is that a key has no identity. It's just a blob of bits.
Joe could make a key that says he's Alice, and you'd have no way of knowing.
A certificate is simply the binding of identity information, like a name, company or address, to a public key. What it's worth depends on who stands behind it.
I can make my own certificate in OS X, but anyone could make one claiming to be me.
So someone has to vouch for it.
Like a notary public, who checks your ID before stamping your document.

You generate a key pair and fill in your identity, then sign a "certificate request" with your private key. That proves to the certificate authority that you own the private key matching the public key you're submitting.
The authority hashes your identity and public key together and signs that with its own private key. That signature is the notary's stamp.
To check it, you need the authority's public key. Browsers and operating systems ship with 30 or 40 of them, valid for decades. VeriSign, Thawte, even the U.S. Postal Service.

beats.title: Certificate chains
beats.t: Today's systems trust over a hundred root certificate authorities. Roots usually sign intermediate certificates, which sign websites' certificates, and browsers check the whole chain. Website certificates are now limited to about a year, and that maximum is shrinking further.
It's mostly automated. Free certificates usually just verify your email address. Paid ones check more.
For GRC's server certificates, VeriSign checks Dun & Bradstreet, plus a fax, phone and email loop.
PGP has the "web of trust" instead. A new key starts untrusted, and as people who know you sign it, its trust grows. Hence key-signing parties.
It's a bit like Google ranking a page by the pages linking to it.
Thanks to this series I get lots of encrypted mail. I'm sure the NSA is watching closely.
Right now using encryption is a red flag. If everyone uses it, it's just an envelope. If everyone else sent postcards, your envelope would look suspicious.
That wraps up the crypto fundamentals. In future episodes we'll cover how SSL, PGP and S/MIME work in detail.

quiz.q: Why can't attackers just keep a table of all 512-bit primes?
options: There are more of them than atoms in the known universe
quiz.explain: The prime number theorem shows big primes are plentiful.

quiz.q: How does factoring difficulty grow as RSA keys get longer?
options: About 1.035 times harder per added bit, which compounds hugely
quiz.explain: Unlike symmetric brute force, each bit adds less, but 512 more bits still means millions of years.

quiz.q: Why is splitting a 128-bit key into two 64-bit halves for two trustees a bad idea?
options: Each trustee then needs only 64 more bits, which is brute-forceable
quiz.explain: Partial keys reduce the remaining secret to a dangerous size.

quiz.q: In Steve's geometry explanation of secret sharing, what do two trustees' points determine?
options: A line whose y-axis crossing is the key
quiz.explain: One point allows infinite lines; two fix it. Three points fix a parabola.

quiz.q: What is a certificate, at its core?
options: Identity information bound to a public key and signed by someone who vouches for it
quiz.explain: Its value depends on who signed it, like a notary's stamp.
